Hi there,

can confirm the exact behavior with RabbitMQ 3.9.13, Celery 3.1.25 / Celery 4.4.7 and Python 3.7.3. Anyone knows a workaround?

Kind regards
Adrian

We have further investigated this issue and the ResultConsumer does not connect back to RabbitMQ.
After the broker restarts and the first message is published to the broker a new queue with the same name as before the restart is created but this time with no consumer subscribed to it.

If you need further information to investigate the issue, please reach out so we can provide more information.

Confirming same behavior with RabbitMQ 3.9.15, Celery 5.2.6 on Python 3.8. 

To reproduce:
#### RabbitMQ
```
$ docker run -d -p 5679:5672 --name rabbitmq-testnode rabbitmq:3.9.15
```
(takes about half a minute for the container to be ready) then configure rabbitmq
```
$ docker exec -it rabbitmq-testnode /bin/bash -c "rabbitmqctl add_user user password; rabbitmqctl set_user_tags user  user_tag administrator; rabbitmqctl add_vhost user_vhost; rabbitmqctl set_permissions -p user_vhost user '.*' '.*' '.*'"
```
#### Consumer
A consumer with only one shared task a_task
```
# consumer.py
from celery import Celery
celery = Celery(
    broker="pyamqp://user:password@127.0.0.1:5679/user_vhost",
    backend="rpc://",
    include=[
        "consumer_tasks",
    ],
)
```
```
# consumer_tasks.py
from celery import shared_task
import time
 
@shared_task()
def a_task():
    return "this is a_task's response"
```
consumer is started with
```
$ celery -A consumer worker -l info --purge
```
#### Producer
```
# producer.py
from celery import Celery
import time

TIMEOUT = 5

celery_app = Celery(
    broker="pyamqp://user:password@127.0.0.1:5679/user_vhost",
    backend="rpc://",
)
celery_app.conf.broker_pool_limit = None #otherwise when broker is down apply_async() hangs until broker is back up

while True:
    try:
        task_signature = celery_app.signature("consumer_tasks.a_task")
        async_result = task_signature.apply_async()
        print(f"-->{async_result.id=}")
        result = async_result.get(TIMEOUT)
        print(f"task result --> {result}")

    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"{exc=} ")
    finally:
        time.sleep(0.5)
        print("")
```
Start the producer
```
$ python producer.py
```
after a couple of seconds (timing is not important) kill the rabbitMQ container
```
$ docker rm -f rabbitmq-testnode
```
then (timing is not important) start rabbitMQ again 
```
$ docker run -d -p 5679:5672 --name rabbitmq-testnode rabbitmq:3.9.15
```
(takes about half a minute for the container to be ready) then configure rabbitmq
```
$ docker exec -it rabbitmq-testnode /bin/bash -c "rabbitmqctl add_user user password; rabbitmqctl set_user_tags user  user_tag administrator; rabbitmqctl add_vhost user_vhost; rabbitmqctl set_permissions -p user_vhost user '.*' '.*' '.*'"
```

Both processes are started when the broker is up and running, then at some point the rabbitMQ container is killed, then rabbitMQ is started and configured again, while the producer and the consumer processes keep running. What is of interest here are the ids of the tasks that get queued _**after**_ the broker is back up again
```
4a186b22-ec09-4210-9239-4e9dbaf37891
86afda7c-0b23-4aaa-96dc-57ad4b116eda
5a72ca88-29e7-4820-afcd-9e786331c02c
0194a9c4-0928-4971-8173-b972867e38cb
31c92db1-b534-4adf-9c81-618acbf3832a
```
These tasks' ids are logged in both processes (producer and consumer) but the consumer reports them as `succeeded`, when the producer reports them as timed out (`TimeoutError('The operation timed out.')`). So, task queuing and consuming is successfully resumed after restarting the broker but the results are not returned correctly to the client/producer.

issue.title: Fix/mip 575/celery open many connections

repository.name: exaflow
repository.description: An orchestration platform for federated learning

issue.body:
fix for [MIP-575](https://team-1617704806227.atlassian.net/browse/MIP-575), [MIP-574](https://team-1617704806227.atlassian.net/browse/MIP-574), [MIP-595](https://team-1617704806227.atlassian.net/browse/MIP-595)

1. At all times there is only one `Celery` object per node in the system. This logic is implemented by a `CeleryAppFactory` class in `mipengine/controller/celery_app.py`

2. Due to bug(s) in the Celery framework (my posts [1](https://github.com/celery/celery/discussions/7474#discussion-4021273),[2](https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/6912#issuecomment-1107260087) on celery's github) if the broker (rabbitmq) would go down and up again, although the tasks would continue to be successfully queued and processed by the consumer celery app, the result would not be returned to the producer celery app until a new `Celery` instance is created on the producer side. A workaround for this problem is implemented in the `CeleryWrapper` class in `mipengine/controller/celery_app.py`, where a new `Celery` object is instantiated when specific exceptions are raised and caught, indicating rabbitmq went down.

3. The controller layer has to execute 3 different actions without any one of them waiting for the other. These actions are 1.repeatedly check which nodes are available (and check what data they contain, Node Landscape Aggregator) at any time, 2.execute algorithms and 3.repeatedly clean database artifacts(tables,views etc.) created during algorithms' execution and are not needed anymore (Cleaner, `mipengine/controller/cleaner.py`). Up until now these were handled by a mix of `asyncio` and threading which was becoming a mess. Implementing these using the `asyncio` framework would be the most efficient approach but it would need some refactoring. Leaving that for a future task I removed all unnecessary `asyncio` usage and moved solely to threads which makes the code much simpler. 
More specifically:
     - `NodeLandscapeAggregator`: `start` method starts executing the `_update` in a new thread, updating the information about the nodes participating in the federation at any point
     - `Cleaner`: `start` method starts executing the `_cleanup_loop` method in a new thread, repeatedly checking if there are artifacts to be dropped and if so queues the relevant tasks to the nodes
     - Algorithm execution (initiated in `Controller`): Each algorithm execution is essentially comprised by a series of task queuing for the nodes to execute and return the results. Each algorithm execution is queuing tasks on a separate thread. Nevertheless, in the case of the algorithm execution although each algorithm is executed on a separate thread of a `Threadpool`, the control is yield to the event loop by using the `run_in_executor` method along with `await`.

body: Any updates on this one? It's a pretty important problem. If the rabbitmq restarts the celery app becomes useless with no way of knowing how to recover the tasks already queued.

I've seen this happen several times on first startup. In my case the virtual host is created by my web server when it starts. Apparently, the worker tries to connect before vhost access is fully configured. So it's essentially a race condition.

The worker really ought to keep trying IMO, and not just fail with an exception. It shouldn't depend on rabbitmq being ready before it starts.

This is one reason why I dislike the model of using decorators with with a global app declaration, passed as an argument to the `celery` command. There's no way to handle exceptions that occur in the program at startup. It's fine under some conditions, but I'd really love to see more support/documentation for a pure python approach. 

Example:

- Create celery app object
- Explicitly add tasks as code objects, rather than implicitly with decorators. 
- Start the application in a try block that can handle exceptions

It's, of course, possible, but it feels a bit sketchy when it's not documented as an alternative.
